recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say which rule applies and what the final expression tidies to.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Apply the product rule
steps.margin_note: First mark. This is a product of two functions written side by side, not one function inside another, so the product rule applies and not the chain rule.
steps.memory_tip: Two separate functions multiplied means the product rule: first times the derivative of the second, plus second times the derivative of the first.
lines: Let y = eˣ(x² + 1). This is a product, so take u = eˣ and v = x² + 1

recall.must_convey: That the product rule is used with u = eˣ and v = x² + 1, giving eˣ(2x) + (x² + 1)eˣ.
accept: use the product rule because two functions are multiplied
first into derivative of second plus second into derivative of first
e power x times two x plus x squared plus one times e power x
rendu functions multiply avuthunnayi kabatti product rule
u dv by dx plus v du by dx

steps.why: Choosing the right rule is the mark. eˣ is not inside (x² + 1) and (x² + 1) is not inside eˣ — they simply multiply — so the chain rule has nothing to act on here.
common_mistakes: Differentiating each factor separately and writing eˣ · 2x as the whole answer.
Using the chain rule as though (x² + 1) were the exponent.

steps.label: Take eˣ common and tidy
steps.margin_note: Second mark. eˣ is a factor of both terms. What is left is x² + 2x + 1, which is a perfect square, so the answer can be written as eˣ(x + 1)².
steps.memory_tip: x² + 2x + 1 is (x + 1)². Spotting the perfect square turns a three-term bracket into a short final line.

recall.must_convey: That eˣ is taken common to give eˣ(x² + 2x + 1), and that x² + 2x + 1 = (x + 1)².

steps.why: Both forms are correct, but the perfect square is the shortest true statement of the answer and shows the working was carried to the end.
common_mistakes: Adding the terms as eˣ(2x + x²) and dropping the 1.
Writing (x + 1)² as x² + 1 when expanding back to check.

insider_note: Product rule, then take eˣ out of both terms. The bracket comes to x² + 2x + 1, a perfect square, so the answer tidies to eˣ(x + 1)².
